title: Repointing a stone boundary wall with lime mortar
subtitle: Rake out weathered mortar joints in a stone garden wall and repoint with a lime mortar that allows moisture movement and remains flexible
excerpt: How to repoint a stone boundary wall with lime mortar. Covers raking out old mortar, wetting the wall section, mixing a suitable lime mortar, pressing and pointing the joints, and brushing to the correct profile.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK Heritage Alliance and Historic England guidance on lime mortars (open access). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A masonry mortar made from lime (either hydraulic lime NHL 2, NHL 3.5, or NHL 5, or non-hydraulic lime putty) mixed with sharp sand, without Portland cement. It remains flexible, allows water vapour to pass through, and can be raked out and replaced without damaging the stone. It sets by carbonation (absorbing CO2 from the air) rather than by chemical hydration.

The process of raking out deteriorated mortar from masonry joints to a minimum depth of 20 to 25 mm and refilling with fresh mortar to re-seal the joint and restore the pointing profile. Repointing extends the life of the masonry and prevents water tracking behind the stones.

The setting mechanism of lime mortar: calcium hydroxide in the mortar absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and converts to calcium carbonate, which is hard and durable. The process requires air access and takes weeks to months to complete fully. Very thick lime mortar joints must be applied in layers to allow carbonation to proceed.

content.text: Old lime mortar between the stones of a garden boundary wall weathers and crumbles away over decades.

replaces the lost mortar with a fresh lime mix that stays flexible, allows moisture movement, and does not trap water the way cement does. BEGINNER: patient raking and careful filling; no specialist tools needed.

Use a cold chisel and club hammer or a sharp filling knife to rake out the deteriorated mortar to a minimum depth of 20 to 25 mm. The joint must be clean and free of loose material before the new mortar goes in. Do not use an angle grinder: on stone walls it damages the stone faces. Brush out all dust from the joint with a stiff brush.
Dampen the masonry surface and joint faces well with clean water before applying fresh
. Dry stone draws moisture from the mortar too quickly and prevents the setting process. In hot or windy weather, wet the surface two or three times over 30 minutes to get adequate saturation.

Mix a 1:2.5 lime to sharp sand ratio using NHL 3.5 hydraulic lime for an exposed garden wall. Mix dry first, then add water gradually until the mortar is stiff enough to hold its shape on the trowel without slumping. A firmer mix is easier to work into deep joints without it dropping out. Pre-mixed lime mortar is available and is a reliable option for small areas.

Pack the mortar into each joint in layers no thicker than 15 mm. For deep joints, fill, scratch, allow to stiffen, then add the next layer. Fill to just proud of the stone face, then run the back of the trowel or a pointing key along the joint to give the final profile. A slightly recessed weatherstruck or flush joint is correct for a stone garden wall; avoid a proud, overfilled joint that channels rain onto the stone face.

to set properly. Cover the fresh work with hessian or polythene in hot, dry, or frosty weather. Do not apply lime mortar when frost is forecast within 24 hours. Keep the new joints slightly damp for the first few days by misting.

attrs.symptom: Mortar dries very fast and crumbles in the joint
attrs.cause: The masonry was too dry before applying, or the weather was hot and windy.
attrs.fix: Dampen the wall thoroughly and keep it damp during application. Work in the shade or on a cool, overcast day.

attrs.symptom: Mortar drops out of the joint before setting
attrs.cause: The mix was too wet and sank under its own weight, or the joint was too wide for a single pass.
attrs.fix: Mix stiffer and pack in layers rather than trying to fill a deep joint in one pass. Allow each layer to stiffen before adding the next.
